title: Is a Post-American World Inevitable?
author: Kurt M. Campbell
text: Podcast Is a Post-American World Inevitable?A Conversation With Kurt Campbell, Rush Doshi, and Mark Leonard Published on August 20, 2026 Play Listen to the Episode 78 minutes 00:00 / 1:18:22 0.5×1×1.5×2× MP3 Close audio player Print Print this article Save Sign in and save to read later Close Share Is a Post-American World Inevitable? A Conversation With Kurt Campbell, Rush Doshi, and Mark Leonard Share in email Share on Facebook Share on X Share on LinkedIn Article link: https://www.foreignaffairs.com/podcasts/post-american-world-inevitablehttps://www.foreignaffairs.com/podcasts/post-american-world-inevitable Request reprint permissions here.Episode Details Ever since Donald Trump returned to the White House last year, a big question has loomed over any discussion of global politics: How much of the change he has brought to U.S. foreign policy, and to the international system, will endure beyond this presidential term?Two essays that open the new issue of Foreign Affairs offer different answers to that question. Kurt Campbell and Rush Doshi, both senior officials in the Biden administration, argue that the U.S. alliance system will not just survive Trump but can emerge stronger, even better suited to countering China and its partners. Mark Leonard, the director of the European Council on Foreign Relations, argues that policymakers in allied capitals and beyond must accept that the United States has fundamentally changed—and get ready to survive a more turbulent and contested world.Dan Kurtz-Phelan wanted to bring Campbell, Doshi, and Leonard together in one conversation to lay out and test these contrasting arguments. They spoke on August 12 about possible futures for U.S. foreign policy—and what those paths mean for a global order built by a very different United States.Sources:“How Alliances Survive” by Kurt M. Campbell and Rush Doshi“The Abandoned Order” by Mark LeonardThis episode of The Foreign Affairs Interview was produced by Elise Burr and Kanishk Tharoor, with audio engineering by Christopher Koch and Markus Zakaria and original music by Robin Hilton. Special thanks to Irina Hogan.This is a rough transcript of the conversation. Please consult the underlying audio prior to citation.DAN KURTZ-PHELANKurt, Rush, Mark, thanks to you all for being here. We were thrilled to have your essays leading off our new issue. “How Alliances Survive” is the piece by Kurt and Rush, and “The Abandoned Order” is Mark’s. Both are fascinating in their own right. And they’re also fascinating, I think, when read together, in part because of the tensions between the arguments but also because of some intriguing echoes. So I’m thrilled to have all three of you here together.KURT CAMPBELLThank you very much, Dan.RUSH DOSHIThanks, Dan.MARK LEONARDThank you.DAN KURTZ-PHELANRush, let me start with you on your piece with Kurt. You two make a case for optimism about U.S. alliances and the alliance system more broadly. That case is surprising not just in light of the dominant headlines about alliances in the last year and a half, but also because you two served on the Biden National Security Council so, politically speaking, you’d be expected to indulge in pretty full-throated predictions of doom at this point. What does the pessimism that nothing will ever be the same in these relationships and hedging will erode alliances over time and trust will never come back? And you know the arguments. What does that pessimism get wrong?RUSH DOSHIWell, let me just start with what I think is clear to everybody, which is that it’s undeniable, the damage done to the alliances in the last 18 months has exceeded what was done in the whole first term of President Trump’s administration, way back. I think a lot of the commentary, I think this is the argument Kurt and I would make: A lot of it tends towards fatalism and despair that we think may be premature. That fatalism is driven by a real sense of grievance. I think the alliances, for many, are over or they won’t ever recover. But I think, for us, that sense of grievance may not be the best analytical, empirical way to think about what comes next.And what we’re trying to do is not diminish the concerns that exist, but maybe contextualize them a bit better because we’re worried that if it hardens into conventional wisdom, if that despair becomes accepted widely, then it risks becoming a self-fulfilling prophecy where policymakers who are convinced that the alliances can’t be saved stop doing the work, essentially, to save them. And basically our argument has three large components. We argue first that the alliance system has weathered a lot of forgotten shocks that are at least as serious as many of these, with one major exception, and that the present circumstances we’re experiencing owe a lot more to presidential personality than to a kind of durable new politics that will change the way America does alliances forever.And we can go into some of the details there but if you look across even our Cold War history, from the Suez crisis of the ‘50s to the debates about French participation in NATO in the ‘60s, where they pushed the U.S. essentially out of France for a while, to some of the challenges in the ‘70s, like the Plaza Accord in the ‘80s, and the ‘70s decision to go off the gold standard. All of that combined, those are real major shocks that I think are worth taking into account.We’ve weathered shocks like those before. Maybe some of the ones we’re seeing today should be seen in that history. And there are many, many others. The collapse of the Soviet Union was foretold to being the end of the alliance system, and that didn’t happen. Even in Asia, where there’s a lot of distrust about U.S. alliances after Saigon, there was a sense that maybe everybody should go nuclear. That didn’t happen. And of course those alliances look stronger. So the history we think is important.Second, we have this deep feeling that the threats that gave rise to these alliances haven’t really faded. In many ways, those threats have intensified and perceptions between the U.S., Europe, and many of its allies are at least converging on elements of that threat, even though there are some disagreements within the Trump administration. And really it’s on the China-Russia axis or nexus or relationship, where there’s a sense that China’s going to hollow out the industrial base of Europe, hollow out the industrial base of Japan and Korea and Taiwan and the United States. So there’s an economic rationale to work together. And there’s a sense across theaters that China and Russia are posing security challenges not individually but together to Europe and to Asia. And that’s creating some cause for greater conversions.The final point is that there are very powerful gravitational forces that we see pulling allies together, even though some allies are trying very hard to de-risk from Washington. If you think about it economically, this second China shock is also pulling the U.S. and Europe together. Technologically, even as countries try to unwind their dependence on the United States, there’s still new dependencies being created in AI and cloud. And then, in the military sense, everybody’s pursuing a defense buildup. Well, the U.S. is a key component of that defense buildup, even as there’s de-risking. So these mega trends, if you will, pull countries together even though they may be trying to pull apart.And beneath the surface, quiet professional bureaucracies are moving forward with a lot of initiatives beyond the glare of politics, beyond the glare of incrimination. I think I’d end with this: We’re not making the case that we can go back. We’re not making the case that everything’s fine. We’re not making the case for restoration. We’re making the case for what we think is pragmatism given this environment of fatalism, that the alliances will endure. And the question really is whether they will evolve for new challenges in the period ahead.And we’d like folks to be thinking harder about what that agenda is going to be. We’re at a moment now, and I’ll end with this, where I think the ball is in the air for what American policy and allied policy will be. We’re thinking about what comes after Trump. And in this environment, it’s worth considering what the ally structure could become rather than just assume that maybe that structure is a relic of the past.DAN KURTZ-PHELANKurt, let me ask you to pick up where Rush left off. I think there’s an element of your piece that is perhaps even more surprising than the case against pessimism, and that’s the case for relative optimism about what the alliance system can look like and achieve over a 10-year period, if you would. If you look beyond Trump, you argue that, ultimately, the real increase in allied capability does come in part because of the anxiety that Trump has induced and the pressure that he’s put on allies actually will put the system in a pretty good position to evolve into the kind of structure that you and Rush and your colleagues were trying to build in the Biden years. What’s the case that optimistic path as in fact possible? It’s not just that we shouldn’t be fatalistic, but there’s actually an opportunity that didn’t look so real even two years ago.KURT CAMPBELLWell, firsthand, again, thank you very much for having us. And Mark, it’s a pleasure to be with you. And look forward to discussing the elements of each of our pieces. So look, I would just simply say we’re using a lot of concepts like optimism, pessimism. I think, at the core of our piece, I think is a realism and a hard-headed recognition both, across the Atlantic and with our Indo-Pacific partners, of the kinds of challenges that are animating the global system, particularly the challenge presented from China in technology, military, overcapacity, and the like. And we believe that that has brought forward a degree of alignment that, in many ways, is unprecedented.I would also just simply say that our piece really is not about resurrecting or going back to the past. It is really a recognition that there are going to be elements of the system are going to survive despite the damage done by Trump. We do not argue that, and we do not in any way excuse the steps that the Trump administration have taken, but we also underscore that some of those concerns preceded Trump. And we’ve seen it over a longer period of time. We’ve argued that what’s necessary is to abandon certain kind of paternalistic, uneven partnerships in which both parties commit to doing more, both the United States and allies and partners.One of the points we make in our piece, Dan, is that Trump has argued for other partners to do more so we can do less. That’s not the equation we’re looking for. We’re asking for both to double down on greater cooperation and technology and munitions and intelligence sharing across the board. And we believe that’s the path that’s necessary going forward. We also argue, one of the things that you’ve seen is this clarion call for middle powers coming together.In truth, the United States has called for middle powers to take a larger share of responsibility, to work more closely together. We’re seeing that in India, in Canada, in Europe, in Japan. New alliances and formations forming. However, each of these countries are also seeking in their own way to deepen relations with the United States.And we believe in a different and new conception, that those partnerships can be empowered with the United States continuing to play a role. And then just lastly, just an anecdote, Dan, to the very good point Rush made. I was at NATO not long ago. I was in one hall in which the political leaders were listening to a Trump administration official berate them. You could see the hostility and the distrust. You walked down the hall to sort of a lesser group of bureaucrats, and they’re busily doing the work of the alliance outside of the glare of this sort of public, insult-driven dynamic. And so we believe that the true deep state is busy basically sustaining habits of cooperation and elements of engagement between the United States and its key partners, because it is one of the clearest elements of bipartisan commitment that continues into this very difficult age.DAN KURTZ-PHELANI want to go to Mark in a second but, Kurt, let me stick with you on just one point. You were one of the people who, when the Biden administration started in 2021 and over the next four years, was charged with really shoring up U.S. alliances after another tense period in the first Trump term. As you guys say in the piece, and Rush said earlier, this time has been different and worse in that regard. But you were in the White House as the top Asia official, and you were deputy secretary of state. As you were trying to rebuild alliances and reassure allies, what were those conversations like? And as you encountered skepticism about the reliability of the U.S., what was most difficult to overcome in that regard?KURT CAMPBELLLook, I think in many respects, Dan, you have to separate the rhetoric from the reality. In almost all the meetings that we had initially were just outpouring of disappointment, concerns, anxieties, insults, attacks against the United States for our lack of credibility and departing from historical norms and values. The hardest thing and the most important thing I would communicate to a new team that is going to come to power, if we’re lucky, in the next three years, is that they’re going to hear a lot of that and they’re going to have to basically power their way through it to key arenas of cooperation that were basically based in self-interests of both sides, and that some of the sentiment that surrounds these negotiations and discussions will be hostile and difficult. And it would be great to resume and recapture a higher degree of trust and the kind of kumbaya spirit that at times, only at times, has animated our relationship with our allies and partners. But to recognize most clearly that you’ve got to be hard-headed and thick-skinned and recognize that we’re doing this together because it is in all of our best interests.And I think that’s probably the biggest lesson I learned. But in almost every endeavor, whether it was AUKUS or The Quad, or the trilateral engagement with partners in Japan and South Korea, or work that we did with Europe behind the scenes on what Russia and China were doing together. Maybe initial quibbles and quarrels, but very quickly getting down to the business of the actual arenas of cooperation. And at the core of our piece is that those areas have expanded and demand more allied work together than probably ever before in our history.DAN KURTZ-PHELANSo fewer gauzy, soaring speeches and more boring long meetings in conference rooms, essentially?KURT CAMPBELLYeah.DAN KURTZ-PHELAN:Mark, before we get into the substance of your piece, which is not exactly what the alliance has been about, about world without order, about all these structures breaking down. I am interested in your response on alliances. You spend much of your time in Europe and talking to European policymakers, and you’ve also lived in and written on Asia in the past. What do you see as plausible or not in the case against pessimism that Kurt and Rush make?MARK LEONARDI think Kurt and Rush are both really inspiring thinkers, but also were amazing practitioners and managed to build a level of understanding and ethic of corporation on Asia where we’ve had no track record between Europeans and Americans during the Cold War, and to knit together the different alliances across different theaters. And it’s really very, very impressive, what they managed to do, but... And I do think that there certainly was a huge desire in European countries and in Asian countries after the Biden administration came back to power, after Trump’s first term, to make the alliances much stronger, to knit them together in new ways, to expand them away from the traditional areas where they were working into new geoeconomics and technology and all sorts of other areas. And it was a very inspiring and exciting agenda.But I fear that having Trump elected twice does mean that nobody is ever going to be able to think about alliances in the same way that they did in the past.There isn’t a single country in Europe, apart from maybe France, that feels any schadenfreude about the state of the Transatlantic alliance. And at the moment, when there are NATO summits I get text messages from different European leaders, panicking about what’s going to happen. The whole mise-en-scène of these events is all about stopping disastrous things from taking place rather than actually achieving anything together.There’s zero trust in the relationship. And the messages are about the U.S. providing less and less to Europeans and asking for more and more alignment in areas which sometimes go against their direct interests. Even under the Biden administration, because the U.S. has so many other priorities, the amount of energy and attention that gets put into getting into a place that’s conducive to European interests on third issues is kind of shrinking. So I think that the U.S., as its attention shifts to other parts of the world, as it becomes harder and harder to achieve things, is going to find it very, very difficult to maintain the kind of virtuosic alliance management that Rush and Kurt were able to do when they were serving in the administrations.And on the other side, there is some very, very expensive hedging that’s taking place. So the good scenario would be that you’d get much more capable allies and that the alliances are much stronger and that Europeans are actually able to pull their weight and able to make a meaningful contribution rather than being sort of vassalized and infantilized kind of whingy partners, that they can actually do something.But I think there’s so much damage done that we’re going to be in a very, very different place. And certainly when I talk to other people in Asia, people are saying out loud now things that they would maybe think privately but would never express. I heard a former Japanese national security adviser say, “I’m not sure if the U.S. will be there for us if we have a kind of problem.” Which is a pretty extraordinary situation, for a Japanese diplomat to be saying things like that on the record in public. And that’s before we get to allies in the Middle East, who might not have great alternatives, but they are extraordinarily destabilized.And there are tensions between these different alliances. What we’re seeing increasingly is that there is a bleed-across from the security situation in one theater to another. And I think where Kurt and Rush were very successful was finding ways of making that into a positive thing. So on Ukraine for example, getting Korea and Japan to play a very important part in managing the Ukraine situation. But I think that’s not a given. I think we could see these different theaters pulling in different directions and creating real security dilemmas for a lot of countries. And I’m not sure that the U.S., in the future, is either going to have the wherewithal or the bandwidth or the public support to really invest in turning these alliances into things which can solve problems for other countries.It doesn’t mean the alliances will disappear, but I fear there’ll be a kind of thinning out of the agenda for cooperation. It’s clear that Japan and India and the U.S. will always share a lot of interest in common when it comes to managing China, and that’s not going to disappear, but I think they will become more transactional than they have been in the past, and maybe more in tension with one another.DAN KURTZ-PHELANJust lingering on the point you made earlier in your answer on hedging, I think in some ways this comes down to the question of whether hedging that is happening over the course of the Trump administration, and presumably subsequently, causes irreversible changes or not. As you talk to policymakers in European and Middle Eastern and Asian capitals, where do you see hedging that may in fact have irreversible effects? Or what kind of hedging do you think may have irreversible effects?MARK LEONARDSome of it might end up being positive. But if you take Denmark for example, which is maybe one of the most extreme countries, they didn’t really have a kind of indigenous military. They basically tried to create a series of spare parts for expeditionary missions, which the U.S. led in different places, and they wanted to be able to plug in and be useful to these things. And they’re now having to kind of rethink their entire position from the ground up. They’re going to be much more focused on territorial defense and on their own priorities. And they’re literally having to rethink absolutely everything from a kind of doctrinal perspective, from a strategy perspective in terms of where their spending goes, who they sign contracts with. But you’re having similar things, maybe not to that extent given that Greenland was a particularly... Well, it was an extraordinary and, I think, unique situation. But you are having similar processes being undertaken by a lot of other countries.And basically, you’re moving from a situation where countries saw themselves within the context of an alliance system. And how do we plug and play and make it all about interoperability with American grand strategy? Towards one where the primary goal is, how do we hedge and how do we make sure that we can defend ourselves if America isn’t there? So you’ll make very, very different choices. In three, four, five years you probably won’t notice much difference. But if you see that going on for five, 10, 15, 20 years... And also, if you do see large amounts of money. Germany’s going to spend 500 billion euros on this over the next period of time. Once you start doing that over a long period of time. Germany will be spending as much as France and the UK combined by 2029.So if you start to make sovereign decisions about that, and you don’t just think about yourself as operating within a U.S. alliance system but developing different kind of relationships, it’s clear that you will just have a different sort of structure. And if that’s happening at a time when the U.S. is actually able to offer less within each individual theater as a result of burgeon shifting to other powers, then their willingness to be flexible and to bend towards the priorities of an administration in Washington will also be altered. If they’re more autonomous, less dependent in their own theater, then they’ll still do things. If there is a very strong alignment of interest, I’m sure that that will work very, very well. But the question is how much people are thinking about the West or about their alliance with the U.S. as the main prism through which they look at the world or whether it’s just one of many relationships. And I think that that is the direction of travel.DAN KURTZ-PHELANMark, before we get deeper into your piece, let me just go back to Kurt and Rush, just to respond. I think there are probably two points that are worth addressing, both the hedging point and what the U.S. will look like in the future point that you made, Mark. Rush, on hedging, I’d be curious how you see the risk that Mark is raising there, that some of these decisions will create, essentially, path dependence that will, over 10 or 15 years, take us to a very different place.RUSH DOSHIWell, thanks, Dan. And I think Mark makes a lot of sense with what he’s offering here. There’s definitely this hedging behavior going on. But what I want to do is bring back hedging in the context of history because I think it’s helpful to take a look at the last 20, 25 years post-Cold War period as itself anomalous. This was a period of alliance cohesion, which was unique. But if we go back to the history of alliances during the Cold War, when we faced an existential challenge, you saw a lot more acrimony than I think people remember.And I think if you look at hedging from that perspective, then it doesn’t seem as much as a departure from broader historical norms. Let me just give you a few examples. I mentioned earlier, in the 1950s we had a Suez crisis. The U.S. essentially threatened to sink the British pound over British foreign policy. We forget that, but that was an enormously consequential action. Again, in the 1960s you have France essentially withdraw from NATO’s unified command and expel a large number of American troops. Nothing like that has happened this time around, even though we’ve had big problems.In the ‘70s, it’s now forgotten, but the U.S. Congress multiple times almost voted to cut U.S. forces in Europe by 50%. That was the Mansfield Amendment. And the Nixon administration, of all administrations, had to fight back against the amendment to kill it. And Mansfield kept pushing it, later, of course, a famous statesman and diplomat. But at the time, somebody who wanted to bring the troops home. And that’s on the security side. But if you look at the economic side again, just a few examples. I mentioned earlier, going off the gold standard. That not coordinated with allies and partners at all. Arguably a more significant international economic decision than these very loophole-filled tariffs, which then have been overturned by the courts. And yet we overcame that problem, too.And actually, when we went off the gold standard we put a 10% tariff on everybody, and still the economic system kind of endured. Plaza in the 1980s is very unique. We pushed Japan and Germany to revalue their currencies. The amount of effect that had on Japan’s exports was far larger than the current tariffs we have now. The appreciation of the Yen was multiples more than the tariff change even today. So what’s the point of all that? The point is the history of alliances has often been a little acrimonious. There’s been protests, like over the Purchasing II deployments, in which millions took to the streets. And the hedging behavior we’re seeing now, in many cases, is a departure not from long historical norms, but from a relatively recent trend of very close interaction. And not all that hedging, as Mark mentioned, is bad.Some of that hedging is good. So let me give you a quick example. Take the military’s share going to American companies with European defense spending. Until recently, that share was like 50%. From 2022 to 2024, post-Ukraine, half of all European spending went to American companies on defense. Let’s say that number goes down from 50% to 40% or 35%. Is that a catastrophic decoupling or de-risking from the U.S.? Or is that sensible resilience? If you look at the European effort, especially the German effort to build up defense industrial capacity, a lot of that is financed by American capital. A lot of that is with American companies playing important roles. American parts.The substructure of European military weaponry is still often things like American command and control, link systems like Link 16, et cetera. On the economic side, I feel like Europe is hedging for sure. They’re doing more of these agreements with other middle powers. But look at the trade statistics. The biggest trend in the last five years is that European exports to China have fallen by like 30%. They’ve gone up to the United States by 15%. And the same is true of Korea and of India as well. So it’s a European and an Asian story. Japan is a bit of an exception. So on the economic side, there’s no choice. If you’re facing an existential challenge from Chinese excess capacity, as Germany is losing 10,000 workers a month, the American market may be your only hope. So you may do some de-risking but, in the end, there’s also greater reliance on the U.S. to be your source of high-margin demand.And finally on tech. There’s definitely efforts by the French and others to stop using Microsoft Office or Zoom, and those are important but, even as they unwind the dependencies of the past, new dependencies are being built around cloud and AI. And some of that’s two-way. The U.S. is highly-dependent on European companies for the AI build-out. There’s no possibility of it without the Dutch or the Germans or the Japanese or the Taiwanese. So again, I think there’s a bit of a de-risking and decoupling in some places, but a recoupling in others.And let me end with one other point, if I may. Just a polling point. I think what Mark paints is a very important picture. There is real anger and grievance. And I think Mark’s organization, ECFR, had a fantastic series of polls across many European countries that are extremely dire. When you see the statistics, countries think of America as an enemy. We can’t disregard that. But I saw one extraordinarily fascinating finding, and you hear it in Asia as well. And that’s that that across, I think, 15 countries polled, in all 15, either a majority or a plurality of those polled thought that, essentially, this too shall pass.That the challenges that we have in the Trump era are a product more of a personality of this one man than of fundamental changes in the U.S. approach to foreign policy. Now, that’s an optimistic hope, but it’s shared by a lot of publics. And I was genuinely shocked when I saw that finding because I think what it shows is people understand perhaps that, down the road, once we turn the page on this era, and this is what the poll captures, the damage is not necessarily permanent. So is there hedging? Yes. But as Kurt mentioned, some of it could be kept capacity-enhancing, some of it is not out of step with historical norms, and not all of it is necessarily going to depart from what we mentioned earlier: There are very real conversions of concern about the China-Russia challenge.KURT CAMPBELLI found much of what Mark said persuasive, and clearly the feel of it. I myself was a student in Great Britain during Reagan’s presidency when we were putting nuclear systems in Europe. I was a young guy but I had real questions about whether the special relationship would survive. Every weekend, hundreds of thousands of people demonstrating tremendous sense of dismay, lack of trust. The major titles on the bestseller list. I remember a book called The Disintegrating West, how it would never survive this period. That was the animating view. And of course we made that through and have seen much more strategic cooperation going forward.I would make one other point. Rush’s examples, they’re all good ones but they’re from Europe. We’ve had a similar dynamic play out in the Indo-Pacific. The period of greatest loss of trust of the United States didn’t come from misbehavior from our chief executive, but failure on the battlefield in Vietnam. In the aftermath of that, many of the countries of Asia felt bereft, absent of hope. Some countries departed on secret nuclear weapons programs in Taiwan and South Korea. President Nixon gave a speech with very little context, the so-called Guam Doctrine, which basically required Asian partners to do much more. In some ways kind of a precursor to some of the sentiment that President Trump has described.Several years later, with the arrival in power of a different president, President Reagan, with a determined and clear outlook, a very strong revival in our partnerships in the Indo-Pacific. So this is not unique to the transatlantic relationship. We have faced these challenges more generally. I would just say one thing, Dan, and I want to commend Foreign Affairs for this: Our larger proposition here is one that, frankly, Rush alluded to just at the end. I think our belief is that, after these elections in the United States, we’re going to see, I think beginning in the fall and winter, a dramatic resurgence in discussion, debate, hope and, frankly, optimism about what comes next.And there’s going to be a lot of discussion about looking two years ahead. I can’t imagine anything worse for President Trump than to be overlooked as people are anticipating the future, but that is exactly what is going to happen. And the hope is, with these essays and engagements, that we animate that debate. And our own belief is that, in many respects, we have agency, and some of this is self-fulfilling. I know what Mark is speaking to. There is almost an inverse relationship. If your interlocutor from Europe believes that you are a supporter of Europe and a supporter of alliances, he is much more likely to say the most harsh and horrible things about how this is unrecoverable.And so there is that ironic dynamic here. I do believe that Europe has, in public opinion polling, is onto something that Rush laid out, in which they are already anticipating the future. And they see this leadership as increasingly personalistic and that, more and more, the subtle signaling, although sometimes pathetic from Republicans and others, is that we’re not on board for seizing Greenland. In fact, much of what President Trump is involved in is really not about an agenda for the future.DAN KURTZ-PHELANWe’ll return to my conversation with Kirk Campbell, Rush Doshi, and Mark Leonard after a short break.Mark, I want to focus on a point that is in some ways at the center, or at least a starting point for your essay, and also relates to the point that Kurt just made, and that’s really about the United States. I think you’re not going to say it this uncharitably, but I think one way of applying the argument in your piece to the hopes that a lot of people in the American foreign policy world have for the future of what American policy might look like might look to you like delusional, magical thinking. That you may be able to see us from the outside better than we see ourselves. You argue in the piece that the U.S. is not going to come back as a kind of guarantor of order. It’s not going to support allies in the same way. Why do you see that change as enduring or permanent? And how do you trace the kind of systemic effects of that when it comes to the order more broadly?MARK LEONARDI think that when people talk about world order, they often start with Henry Kissinger, who kind of argues that you have these two pillars for it, which is a commonly agreed set of rules about what states can and can’t do, which people might not love but are at least willing to live with, and then a balance of power which can somehow enforce them and ensure that they take place. And if we think about the order that we’ve had over the last period of time, we did have those two things. And the U.S. was the kind of central glue which both helped to develop those rules and then also to enforce them. And America isn’t going away. It’s still the preeminent military, economic, and technological power in the world. But it is changing in quite a fundamental way as the balance of power in the world changes. And I think it’s increasingly clear that Washington has lost its ability to prevent conflicts, to ensure the free flow of commerce around the world.It can’t even open the Strait of Hormuz. It’s struggled to get the Houthis into line in the Red Sea. And there’s always been asymmetric challenges to American power. Kurt talked about Vietnam earlier. We saw what happened in Afghanistan and places like that. But I think there are a series of technologies which have emerged which make it easier for weaker opponents to create a lot of disruption, as Iran is kind of proving on the one hand. And there also has been a diffusion of power in the world.
